title: Sparse Arrays
directAnswer: Given a list of strings and a list of queries, return for each query how many times it appears in the strings. Don't re-scan all strings per query — that's O(n·q). Build a frequency map (string → count) in one pass over the strings, then answer each query with an O(1) lookup, defaulting to 0 for misses. Total O(n + q).

remember.pattern: Precompute a frequency map, then O(1) lookups
rules: Count **exact** string matches — `'ab'` and `'abc'` are different keys, no prefix or substring logic.
Build the map **once** over `strings`, then each query is a single `O(1)` lookup.
A query absent from the map must return **0**, not null/None — use `getOrDefault` / `dict.get(q, 0)`.
Preserve query order in the output: the i-th answer corresponds to the i-th query.
Strings are case-sensitive and matched in full; don't trim or lowercase unless the prompt says so.
whenToUse: Repeated 'how many times does X appear?' questions over a fixed collection
Many lookups against the same dataset — amortize the scan once
Exact-match counting where a hash map's O(1) average lookup fits
antiSignals: Queries are substring or prefix matches → trie or suffix structure, not a flat frequency map
The collection changes between queries → you'd rebuild or maintain incrementally
You need ranking by frequency, not point lookups → heap or sorted counts
remember.takeaway: When the same dataset is queried many times for exact-match counts, pay O(n) once to build a frequency map, then every query is O(1). The whole skill is recognizing 'count occurrences' equals 'hash map of counts'.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you avoid the naive nested scan and instead precompute counts so repeated queries are cheap — the core 'amortize work into a hash map' instinct.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Looping over every string for every query (O(n·q)), or returning null/None for a query that never appears instead of 0.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Say 'I'll trade O(n) preprocessing for O(1) per query' before coding, and note the exact-match requirement so the interviewer knows you won't accidentally do substring matching.

problemStatement: There is a collection of input strings and a collection of query strings. For each query string, determine **how many times** it occurs in the list of input strings. Return the counts in the **same order** as the queries.
constraints: All strings consist of lowercase English letters
understanding: You have a fixed bag of strings and a separate list of query strings. For each query you report its exact-match occurrence count in the bag. Multiple queries hit the same bag, so it pays to summarize the bag once into counts and then look up each query.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the match exact or a substring/prefix?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Exact full-string match. 'abc' does not count toward a query of 'ab'.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What do I return for a query that never appears?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 0. Use a default-zero lookup so absent keys don't blow up.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the matching case-sensitive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — treat strings exactly as given. The constraints here are all lowercase anyway.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the output order match the query order?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The i-th number answers the i-th query.

examples.explanation: 'aba' appears twice, 'xzxb' once, 'ab' never (it's a substring of others but not an exact match).

approaches.name: Brute Force — Re-scan Strings Per Query
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to establish correctness, then point out the redundant rescanning that the map removes.
hints: The literal approach: for each query, walk the whole strings list and count exact matches.
How many total comparisons is that across q queries and n strings?
Notice you rescan the same unchanged strings list for every query. Can you summarize it once instead?
approaches.complexityReasoning: q queries × n strings (× up to 20 chars per compare) = O(n·q) comparisons; nothing is reused between queries.
approaches.explanation:
For each query, loop over every input string and increment a counter when they match exactly.

**Why it's the natural first attempt.** It mirrors the question directly: 'how many times does this query appear?' becomes 'count the strings equal to this query'. No data structures, just two loops.

**Where the waste is.** The strings list never changes between queries, yet we walk all of it again for each one. With `n` strings and `q` queries that's `n·q` string comparisons. For the constraints (both up to 1000) that's a million comparisons — survivable here, but the moment either grows, it balloons. More importantly, it signals you didn't spot the reuse.

**The fix in one sentence.** Summarize the unchanging strings list *once* into a count table, then each query reads the table in constant time.
approaches.insight: The strings list is read-only across all queries — anything you recompute per query that doesn't depend on the query is wasted work. That observation is the whole reason to precompute.

approaches.name: Frequency Map — Precompute Counts (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer: one pass to count, then O(1) per query.
hints: What structure lets you ask 'how many of this exact string?' in O(1) after a single pass?
Walk strings once, incrementing a map keyed by the string. Then each query is a lookup.
For a query missing from the map, the answer is 0 — use a default-zero accessor.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the map is one pass over n strings: O(n). Each of q queries is an O(1) average lookup: O(q). Total O(n + q); the map holds up to n distinct keys → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Make a single pass over the input strings, tallying each into a hash map keyed by the string. Then answer every query with one map lookup.

**Why one pass beats many.** Every query asks the same kind of question — 'how many copies of this exact string exist?' — about the *same* unchanging collection. So compute all those counts once: a map from string to its occurrence count. After that, the strings list is never touched again.

**Why the default-zero lookup matters.** A query like `'ab'` may never appear in the strings. The map simply has no key for it. Reading a missing key naively returns `null` (Java) or raises `KeyError` (Python). Using `getOrDefault(query, 0)` / `freq.get(query, 0)` returns `0` cleanly — which is exactly the count of a string that never occurs.

**Why this is exact-match by construction.** The map key is the *whole* string. Two strings collide in the same bucket only if they're equal, so `'abc'` and `'ab'` are distinct keys and never cross-count. No extra logic needed to enforce exact matching — the data structure does it.

**Why it scales.** Preprocessing is `O(n)`, each query is `O(1)` average, so `q` queries cost `O(q)`. Compared to the brute force's `O(n·q)`, the saving grows with the number of queries — which is the whole point when many queries hit one dataset.
approaches.insight: Counting occurrences is the textbook hash-map-of-counts pattern. The mental move is 'separate the query-independent work (counting) from the per-query work (lookup)'. Do the expensive part once. The same shape powers anagram grouping, mode finding, and 'first unique character'.

Absent queries default to 0 instead of throwing on a null Integer.

One O(1) lookup per query, preserving order; missing keys yield 0.

edgeCases.behavior: No match — keys are whole strings, so 'ab' ≠ 'aba'.
Each does the same O(1) lookup; the map is built only once.

pitfalls: Returning null/None for an absent query instead of 0.
Building the map inside the query loop, reintroducing O(n·q).
Keying on something other than the whole string and accidentally matching substrings.

commonMistakes: Re-scanning all strings for every query (O(n·q)) instead of precomputing counts.
Returning null/None for a query that never appears instead of 0.
Using == on Strings in Java, comparing references rather than contents.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reference equality in Java
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `==` compares object references; two equal strings can be different objects and the count silently stays 0.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Crashing on absent queries
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A query not in the map has no entry; a plain get returns null (Java) or raises KeyError (Python).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Rebuilding the map per query
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Constructing the frequency map inside the query loop throws away the whole benefit and is back to O(n·q).

patternNote: Precompute a frequency map, then O(1) lookups. When many exact-match count queries hit one fixed dataset, summarize it once (O(n)) and answer each query in O(1). The hash key being the whole string enforces exact matching for free.
